      "title": "Support skill groups and workspace member assignments",
      "url": "https://linear.app/21n/issue/SKI-11/support-skill-groups-and-workspace-member-assignments",
      "description": "## Executive summary\n\nAdd workspace-level skill groups so Skillplane can organize related skills by domain and associate workspace members with those groups\u2014for example Design, Marketing, Development, and Sales.\n\n## Problem or opportunity\n\nA flat workspace skill catalog does not express which skills belong together or which members should work with a domain-specific collection. As the catalog and workspace membership grow, discovery, onboarding, and administration become harder.\n\n## Expected outcome\n\nWorkspace administrators can define reusable skill groups, associate skills and members with them, and inspect those relationships. Members can quickly find the skills relevant to their domains.\n\n## Goals\n\n* Create, rename, describe, archive, and restore skill groups within a workspace.\n* Associate skills with skill groups.\n* Associate workspace members with skill groups.\n* Show and filter skills and members by group.\n* Preserve workspace isolation, role-based administration, auditability, and deterministic API behavior.\n* Define how group membership interacts with skill visibility and authorization before rollout.\n\n## Non-goals\n\n* Replacing existing workspace roles.\n* Inferring a member's group from job title or behavior.\n* Automatically generating or changing skill content.\n* Implementing organization-wide groups shared across unrelated workspaces unless separately designed.\n\n## Acceptance criteria\n\n* A workspace can maintain domain groups such as Design, Marketing, Development, and Sales.\n* Authorized administrators can add and remove skills and members without duplicate associations.\n* Group detail views expose the associated skills and members; skill/member views expose their groups.\n* Lists and search can filter by group.\n* Archived groups do not silently delete skills, members, or historical audit records.\n* Cross-workspace references are rejected.\n* Every membership change is attributable in audit history.\n* Existing workspaces continue to work without creating groups.\n* Product and API semantics clearly state whether groups are organizational only or affect effective skill access.\n\n## Dependencies and risks\n\n* Existing workspace membership, skill visibility, authorization, and audit models.\n* Risk of accidentally widening access if group membership is treated as a grant.\n* Risk of confusing group membership with workspace role or team ownership.\n* Migration and indexing requirements for existing skills and members.\n* Large groups may require pagination and bulk-operation safeguards.\n\n## Open questions\n\n* Does membership grant skill access, configure defaults, or only categorize and filter?\n* Can a skill and a member belong to multiple groups?\n* Who may administer groups: owners only, or admins as well?\n* Should personal workspaces support groups?\n* How should group removal affect effective access, pinned skills, or agent configurations?\n* Are nested groups needed, or should the first version remain flat?\n\n## Supporting documents\n\n* [Ideation & Product Rationale](<https://linear.app/21n/document/ideation-and-product-rationale-ski-11-support-skill-groups-and-72f905b3b2ce>)\n* [Architecture & Delivery Plan](<https://linear.app/21n/document/architecture-and-delivery-plan-ski-11-support-skill-groups-and-daf45bcc1c17>)",

      "identifier": "SKI-1",
      "title": "Move service-principal credential authentication to AuthFn API keys",
      "url": "https://linear.app/21n/issue/SKI-1/move-service-principal-credential-authentication-to-authfn-api-keys",
      "description": "## Context\n\nSkillplane previously owned custom service-principal credential authentication using opaque `sps_...` secrets. AuthFn already provides API-key issuance, hashing, authentication, expiration, and revocation, including a stable API-key actor identity. Skillplane should use that internal capability while continuing to own its service-principal domain model.\n\n## Responsibility split\n\n### AuthFn\n\n* Issue agent credentials.\n* Hash and verify credential secrets.\n* Handle expiration and revocation.\n* Return a stable authenticated actor identity.\n\n### Skillplane\n\n* Map the authenticated actor to a Skillplane service principal.\n* Bind that principal to a workspace.\n* Store and enforce Skillplane-specific roles, scopes, delegation, and domain policy.\n* Record domain audit metadata and lifecycle events.\n* Present credentials to users as Skillplane agent credentials without exposing provider implementation details.\n\nA service principal remains a Skillplane domain entity; only credential lifecycle and authentication are delegated internally.\n\n## Revised product decision\n\nThere is no compatibility window for the former `sps_...` format.\n\n* Removed credentials must fail authentication immediately.\n* The obsolete credential-hash column and fallback verification path must be removed.\n* Existing service-principal records may remain without a usable credential and receive a fresh current credential through the normal rotation action.\n* UI and public service-principal responses must not expose AuthFn provider names, provider enums, or provider-specific identifiers.\n\n## Work\n\n* Define the AuthFn actor-to-Skillplane-service-principal mapping.\n* Replace custom credential verification in the API and MCP authentication paths.\n* Preserve least-privilege workspace, role, scope, delegation, and authorization enforcement.\n* Remove the former credential format, storage, compatibility behavior, migration guide, and migration-as-rotation code.\n* Keep end-user UI and documentation provider-neutral.\n* Avoid exposing raw secrets after the one-time creation or rotation response.\n* Add issuance, authentication, expiration, revocation, removed-format rejection, rotation, authorization, audit, schema, and UI tests.\n* Preserve operator-visible auditability without exposing provider details in the product surface.\n\n## Acceptance criteria\n\n* New agent credentials are issued and authenticated through AuthFn internally.\n* The former `sps_...` credential format is not accepted.\n* `service_principals.credential_hash` and its fallback verification path are removed.\n* Existing service-principal records can receive a fresh current credential through rotation.\n* Skillplane service-principal records continue to own workspace association, role, scopes, delegation, and domain policy.\n* Revoked or expired credentials fail closed.\n* MCP authorization remains least-privilege and is covered by integration and security tests.\n* Credential lifecycle actions remain auditable.\n* The UI and public API do not expose AuthFn provider names or provider-specific identifiers.\n* No raw credential is persisted or returned after its one-time creation or rotation response.",

      "description": "## Executive summary\n\nAfter McpFn publishes the upstream Cloudflare Worker packaging fix, Skillplane must upgrade its McpFn dependencies, remove obsolete or temporary MCP Worker compatibility configuration, and verify the full development topology without changing authentication behavior.\n\n## Problem\n\nSkillplane currently consumes `@mcpfn/auth@0.0.4`, `@mcpfn/core@0.0.4`, and `@mcpfn/testing@0.0.4`. Skillplane also retains `allow_eval_during_startup` alongside compatibility date `2026-05-03`; local workerd rejects that combination because the behavior is already default for dates on or after 2025-06-01.\n\nThe Worker should consume the corrected McpFn release and use current Cloudflare configuration without retaining a permanent Zod alias, compatibility shim, or redundant flag.\n\n## Expected outcome\n\nThe full Skillplane development topology deploy path includes the MCP Worker successfully. Skillplane uses the patched published McpFn packages, generated Wrangler configuration is valid for the configured compatibility date, and existing MCP authentication behavior is preserved.\n\n## Goals\n\n* Upgrade Skillplane to the patched McpFn package release.\n* Remove the obsolete `allow_eval_during_startup` compatibility flag from source and generated MCP Worker configurations.\n* Remove any temporary consumer-side Zod alias or workaround once the upstream package fix is available.\n* Validate the rendered topology, Worker bundle execution, and controlled development deployment.\n* Preserve the existing authenticated MCP endpoint behavior.\n\n## Non-goals\n\n* Implementing the upstream McpFn or MCP SDK packaging correction.\n* Changing Skillplane tool contracts, tenant policy, or authentication semantics.\n* Production deployment as part of backlog capture.\n* Broad dependency modernization unrelated to this failure.\n\n## Acceptance criteria\n\n* Skillplane's lockfile resolves the patched published versions of all required McpFn packages.\n* No permanent Skillplane-local `zod/v4` alias or compatibility shim is required.\n* `allow_eval_during_startup` is absent from the source configuration and all rendered topology configurations.\n* The development topology render and deployment checks pass.\n* A real workerd startup test reaches ready state; validation is not limited to Wrangler dry-run bundling.\n* A controlled full development topology deployment includes the MCP Worker without Cloudflare error 10021 or `Class2 is not a constructor`.\n* Smoke validation confirms the deployed MCP endpoint still requires authentication.\n* Validation results clearly distinguish local workerd, Cloudflare development deployment, and production status.\n\n## Dependencies and risks\n\n* Blocked on the upstream McpFn fix and published package release tracked in MCP-4.\n* Generated Wrangler files must be regenerated from their source templates rather than edited only as outputs.\n* A dependency upgrade could carry unrelated behavior changes;       "identifier": "SKI-11",
      "title": "Support skill groups and workspace member assignments",
      "url": "https://linear.app/21n/issue/SKI-11/support-skill-groups-and-workspace-member-assignments",
      "description": "## Executive summary\n\nAdd workspace-level skill groups so Skillplane can organize related skills by domain and associate workspace members with those groups\u2014for example Design, Marketing, Development, and Sales.\n\n## Problem or opportunity\n\nA flat workspace skill catalog does not express which skills belong together or which members should work with a domain-specific collection. As the catalog and workspace membership grow, discovery, onboarding, and administration become harder.\n\n## Expected outcome\n\nWorkspace administrators can define reusable skill groups, associate skills and members with them, and inspect those relationships. Members can quickly find the skills relevant to their domains.\n\n## Goals\n\n* Create, rename, describe, archive, and restore skill groups within a workspace.\n* Associate skills with skill groups.\n* Associate workspace members with skill groups.\n* Show and filter skills and members by group.\n* Preserve workspace isolation, role-based administration, auditability, and deterministic API behavior.\n* Define how group membership interacts with skill visibility and authorization before rollout.\n\n## Non-goals\n\n* Replacing existing workspace roles.\n* Inferring a member's group from job title or behavior.\n* Automatically generating or changing skill content.\n* Implementing organization-wide groups shared across unrelated workspaces unless separately designed.\n\n## Acceptance criteria\n\n* A workspace can maintain domain groups such as Design, Marketing, Development, and Sales.\n* Authorized administrators can add and remove skills and members without duplicate associations.\n* Group detail views expose the associated skills and members; skill/member views expose their groups.\n* Lists and search can filter by group.\n* Archived groups do not silently delete skills, members, or historical audit records.\n* Cross-workspace references are rejected.\n* Every membership change is attributable in audit history.\n* Existing workspaces continue to work without creating groups.\n* Product and API semantics clearly state whether groups are organizational only or affect effective skill access.\n\n## Dependencies and risks\n\n* Existing workspace membership, skill visibility, authorization, and audit models.\n* Risk of accidentally widening access if group membership is treated as a grant.\n* Risk of confusing group membership with workspace role or team ownership.\n* Migration and indexing requirements for existing skills and members.\n* Large groups may require pagination and bulk-operation safeguards.\n\n## Open questions\n\n* Does membership grant skill access, configure defaults, or only categorize and filter?\n* Can a skill and a member belong to multiple groups?\n* Who may administer groups: owners only, or admins as well?\n* Should personal workspaces support groups?\n* How should group removal affect effective access, pinned skills, or agent configurations?\n* Are nested groups needed, or should the first version remain flat?\n\n## Supporting documents\n\n* [Ideation & Product Rationale](<https://linear.app/21n/document/ideation-and-product-rationale-ski-11-support-skill-groups-and-72f905b3b2ce>)\n* [Architecture & Delivery Plan](<https://linear.app/21n/document/architecture-and-delivery-plan-ski-11-support-skill-groups-and-daf45bcc1c17>)",

      "id": "693fecfe-0647-47d3-a152-20874fb3fad5",
      "identifier": "SKI-1",
      "title": "Move service-principal credential authentication to AuthFn API keys",
      "url": "https://linear.app/21n/issue/SKI-1/move-service-principal-credential-authentication-to-authfn-api-keys",
      "description": "## Context\n\nSkillplane previously owned custom service-principal credential authentication using opaque `sps_...` secrets. AuthFn already provides API-key issuance, hashing, authentication, expiration, and revocation, including a stable API-key actor identity. Skillplane should use that internal capability while continuing to own its service-principal domain model.\n\n## Responsibility split\n\n### AuthFn\n\n* Issue agent credentials.\n* Hash and verify credential secrets.\n* Handle expiration and revocation.\n* Return a stable authenticated actor identity.\n\n### Skillplane\n\n* Map the authenticated actor to a Skillplane service principal.\n* Bind that principal to a workspace.\n* Store and enforce Skillplane-specific roles, scopes, delegation, and domain policy.\n* Record domain audit metadata and lifecycle events.\n* Present credentials to users as Skillplane agent credentials without exposing provider implementation details.\n\nA service principal remains a Skillplane domain entity; only credential lifecycle and authentication are delegated internally.\n\n## Revised product decision\n\nThere is no compatibility window for the former `sps_...` format.\n\n* Removed credentials must fail authentication immediately.\n* The obsolete credential-hash column and fallback verification path must be removed.\n* Existing service-principal records may remain without a usable credential and receive a fresh current credential through the normal rotation action.\n* UI and public service-principal responses must not expose AuthFn provider names, provider enums, or provider-specific identifiers.\n\n## Work\n\n* Define the AuthFn actor-to-Skillplane-service-principal mapping.\n* Replace custom credential verification in the API and MCP authentication paths.\n* Preserve least-privilege workspace, role, scope, delegation, and authorization enforcement.\n* Remove the former credential format, storage, compatibility behavior, migration guide, and migration-as-rotation code.\n* Keep end-user UI and documentation provider-neutral.\n* Avoid exposing raw secrets after the one-time creation or rotation response.\n* Add issuance, authentication, expiration, revocation, removed-format rejection, rotation, authorization, audit, schema, and UI tests.\n* Preserve operator-visible auditability without exposing provider details in the product surface.\n\n## Acceptance criteria\n\n* New agent credentials are issued and authenticated through AuthFn internally.\n* The former `sps_...` credential format is not accepted.\n* `service_principals.credential_hash` and its fallback verification path are removed.\n* Existing service-principal records can receive a fresh current credential through rotation.\n* Skillplane service-principal records continue to own workspace association, role, scopes, delegation, and domain policy.\n* Revoked or expired credentials fail closed.\n* MCP authorization remains least-privilege and is covered by integration and security tests.\n* Credential lifecycle actions remain auditable.\n* The UI and public API do not expose AuthFn provider names or provider-specific identifiers.\n* No raw credential is persisted or returned after its one-time creation or rotation response.",

name: create-pr-ghother
description: Create or update a GitHub pull request using `GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other`, especially when the current worktree is dirty or based on the wrong branch. Use this when the user wants a PR against a specific remote and branch such as `origin/dev` or `next/next`, needs `.conduct` included or excluded based on target, wants branch/title prefixing, or needs a clean temporary worktree to avoid dragging unrelated history into the PR.
---

# Create PR GH Other

## Overview

Use this skill when the user wants a PR created with the `gh-other` GitHub profile and the result must be clean, accurately described, and targeted to a specific remote and branch.

This skill exists to avoid four recurring failure modes:
- pushing from the wrong branch ancestry
- creating vague or misleading PR titles and descriptions
- accidentally including `.conduct` content in the wrong target
- leaking generated/build artifacts because `.gitignore` was not checked before staging

## Required Inputs

- target remote and target branch
  - common: `origin/dev`
  - common: `next/next`
- optional prefix for both branch name and PR title
- the current worktree containing the intended changes

If the user gives only a branch name like `dev`, assume `origin/dev`.
If the user gives only `next`, assume `next/next`.

## Hard Rules

- Always set `GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other` on every `gh` command.
- Do not create forks.
- Do not create extra remotes.
- Push to the provided remote only.
- If permission is denied for that remote/repository, abort and report the denial. Do not fall back to a fork or a different remote.
- If the target is `origin/dev`, do not push `.conduct` contents.
- If the target is `next/next`, include `.conduct` contents.
- Before staging, scan the changed content for files that should be gitignored and update `.gitignore` first.
- Do not generate a PR title/body from guesswork. Read the actual changed files and make the title/body reflect the real scope.

## Workflow

### 1. Inspect The Current Worktree Thoroughly

Start by understanding what actually changed.

Run and inspect at minimum:

```bash
git status --short
git branch --show-current
git remote -v
git fetch <target-remote> <target-branch>
git rev-list --left-right --count <target-remote>/<target-branch>...HEAD
git diff --stat
git diff --name-status
```

Then read the high-signal changed files, not just filenames:

- source files
- tests
- examples
- docs
- package manifests
- `.gitignore`

Do this before drafting the branch name, commit message, PR title, or PR body.

### 2. Decide Whether A Clean Temporary Worktree Is Required

Use the current worktree branch only if it is already a clean PR base for the target branch.

Create a temporary clean worktree from `<target-remote>/<target-branch>` if any of these are true:

- the current branch is far ahead/behind the target branch
- the branch contains unrelated commits
- the user’s changes are mixed into an old branch
- a direct PR from the current branch would drag in unrelated history

When a clean worktree is needed:

1. create a temporary worktree from the target branch
2. replay the user’s intended changes into it
3. use that temporary worktree branch for commit, push, and PR

### 3. Replay Changes Safely

When replaying onto a clean worktree:

- For modified tracked files:
  - prefer patch-based replay over full-file copying
  - preserve upstream target-branch fixes
  - do not overwrite a newer target file wholesale unless the file is clearly example-only or entirely owned by the current change
- For brand-new files and directories:
  - copy them directly
- After replay:
  - run `git status --short`
  - confirm the staged/unstaged set still matches the intended scope

If replay causes conflicts or unexpected test regressions, resolve them before continuing. Do not silently ship the broken replay.

### 4. Apply `.conduct` Policy Before Staging

Target-specific policy:

- `origin/dev`
  - exclude `.conduct` contents from the PR
  - if needed, stage with explicit exclusions rather than hoping they stay out
- `next/next`
  - include `.conduct` contents

Do not decide this ad hoc. The target determines the policy.

### 5. Scan For Gitignore Candidates Before Staging

Before `git add`, inspect the full changed/untracked set for generated or machine-local files.

Check:

```bash
git status --short
git ls-files --others --exclude-standard
```

Common artifacts to catch:

- `node_modules/`
- `.build/`
- `.swiftpm/`
- `DerivedData/`
- `**/xcuserdata/`
- `**/*.xcuserstate`
- build outputs like `dist/`, `build/`, generated `.js`, `.d.ts`, source maps
- temporary verification symlinks
- cache folders created during testing

If ignore rules are missing, update `.gitignore` before staging.

Do not stage generated artifacts and then “remember to remove them later”.

### 6. Stage Only The Intended Scope

After `.gitignore` is correct and the replay is settled:

- stage only the files meant for the PR
- verify `.conduct` inclusion/exclusion again
- verify that no machine-local or generated artifacts are staged

Run:

```bash
git status --short
git diff --cached --stat
```

If a temporary verification helper was added, like a root `node_modules` symlink, remove it before commit unless it is intentionally part of the change.

### 7. Verify On The PR Branch

Run the relevant tests from the branch that will actually be pushed.

Do not rely only on tests run from the original worktree if the PR branch was rebuilt in a temporary worktree.

At minimum, run the tests that match the touched packages or the user’s requested verification scope.

### 8. Create Branch Name, Commit Message, PR Title, And PR Body From The Actual Diff

Branch naming:

- if a prefix is provided, prefix the branch name with it
- otherwise use a concise branch name that reflects the real change

Default branch pattern:

```text
<prefix>/<slug>
```

or, if no prefix is provided:

```text
codex/<slug>
```

Title rules:

- if a prefix is provided, prefix the PR title too
- mention the real primary areas changed
- do not collapse broad runtime work into a narrow feature label

Examples of what the title/body must capture when present:

- `datafn/swift`
- `datafn/swift-bridge`
- `searchfn/swift`
- example apps
- docs and regression coverage

Body rules:

- summarize the real change areas
- mention included packages/directories when the PR is broad
- list the tests actually run
- explicitly note `.conduct` inclusion or exclusion based on target

### 9. Push Using The Provided Remote Only

Derive the repository from the provided remote:

```bash
git remote get-url <target-remote>
```

Push the branch to that remote only.

Preferred approach:

- use the provided remote/repository
- use the `gh-other` auth context for PR creation
- if push permission is denied for that remote, stop and report the denial

Do not:

- add a new remote
- create a fork
- push to a personal repository
- silently change the destination repository

### 10. Create The PR And Verify The Live Metadata

Create the PR with:

- `GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other`
- the requested base remote + branch
- the pushed branch on the provided remote

After creation, immediately inspect the live PR:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh pr view <number-or-url> --json title,body,url,baseRefName,headRefName
```

Confirm that:

- the title matches the real scope
- the body reflects the actual work
- the correct remote/branch were used

If the live title/body are off, fix them before reporting success:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh pr edit ...
```

## Learnings To Carry Forward

- Check branch ancestry before doing anything else. An old branch can make a perfectly valid code change produce a terrible PR.
- Use a clean temporary worktree when the source branch is not a clean base for the target branch.
- Replay tracked file changes as patches whenever possible; full-file copying can wipe out newer target-branch fixes.
- Read enough of the changed files to describe the real work. Titles like “native-backed search” are wrong if the PR actually adds `datafn/swift` core runtime.
- Decide `.conduct` policy from the target branch up front, not at the end.
- Scan for ignore-worthy artifacts before staging. This is when `.build`, `.swiftpm`, `DerivedData`, `xcuserdata`, and verification symlinks are easiest to catch.
- Never stage temporary verification helpers such as `node_modules` symlinks.
- After PR creation, verify the live PR metadata. Do not assume the first draft title/body is good enough.

## Final Response Requirements

When the skill completes, report:

- PR URL
- pushed branch name
- target remote/branch
- whether `.conduct` was included or excluded
- whether `.gitignore` changed and why
- tests run on the pushed branch
- any abort reason if permissions or remote policy blocked completion

# Create PR GH Other

## Overview

Use this skill when the user wants a PR created with the `gh-other` GitHub profile and the result must be clean, accurately described, and targeted to a specific remote and branch.

This skill exists to avoid four recurring failure modes:
- pushing from the wrong branch ancestry
- creating vague or misleading PR titles and descriptions
- accidentally including `.conduct` content in the wrong target
- leaking generated/build artifacts because `.gitignore` was not checked before staging

## Required Inputs

- target remote and target branch
  - common: `origin/dev`
  - common: `next/next`
- optional prefix for both branch name and PR title
- the current worktree containing the intended changes

If the user gives only a branch name like `dev`, assume `origin/dev`.
If the user gives only `next`, assume `next/next`.

## Hard Rules

- Always set `GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other` on every `gh` command.
- Do not create forks.
- Do not create extra remotes.
- Push to the provided remote only.
- If permission is denied for that remote/repository, abort and report the denial. Do not fall back to a fork or a different remote.
- If the target is `origin/dev`, do not push `.conduct` contents.
- If the target is `next/next`, include `.conduct` contents.
- Before staging, scan the changed content for files that should be gitignored and update `.gitignore` first.
- Do not generate a PR title/body from guesswork. Read the actual changed files and make the title/body reflect the real scope.

## Workflow

### 1. Inspect The Current Worktree Thoroughly

Start by understanding what actually changed.

Run and inspect at minimum:

```bash
git status --short
git branch --show-current
git remote -v
git fetch <target-remote> <target-branch>
git rev-list --left-right --count <target-remote>/<target-branch>...HEAD
git diff --stat
git diff --name-status
```

Then read the high-signal changed files, not just filenames:

- source files
- tests
- examples
- docs
- package manifests
- `.gitignore`

Do this before drafting the branch name, commit message, PR title, or PR body.

### 2. Decide Whether A Clean Temporary Worktree Is Required

Use the current worktree branch only if it is already a clean PR base for the target branch.

Create a temporary clean worktree from `<target-remote>/<target-branch>` if any of these are true:

- the current branch is far ahead/behind the target branch
- the branch contains unrelated commits
- the user’s changes are mixed into an old branch
- a direct PR from the current branch would drag in unrelated history

When a clean worktree is needed:

1. create a temporary worktree from the target branch
2. replay the user’s intended changes into it
3. use that temporary worktree branch for commit, push, and PR

### 3. Replay Changes Safely

When replaying onto a clean worktree:

- For modified tracked files:
  - prefer patch-based replay over full-file copying
  - preserve upstream target-branch fixes
  - do not overwrite a newer target file wholesale unless the file is clearly example-only or entirely owned by the current change
- For brand-new files and directories:
  - copy them directly
- After replay:
  - run `git status --short`
  - confirm the staged/unstaged set still matches the intended scope

If replay causes conflicts or unexpected test regressions, resolve them before continuing. Do not silently ship the broken replay.

### 4. Apply `.conduct` Policy Before Staging

Target-specific policy:

- `origin/dev`
  - exclude `.conduct` contents from the PR
  - if needed, stage with explicit exclusions rather than hoping they stay out
- `next/next`
  - include `.conduct` contents

Do not decide this ad hoc. The target determines the policy.

### 5. Scan For Gitignore Candidates Before Staging

Before `git add`, inspect the full changed/untracked set for generated or machine-local files.

Check:

```bash
git status --short
git ls-files --others --exclude-standard
```

Common artifacts to catch:

- `node_modules/`
- `.build/`
- `.swiftpm/`
- `DerivedData/`
- `**/xcuserdata/`
- `**/*.xcuserstate`
- build outputs like `dist/`, `build/`, generated `.js`, `.d.ts`, source maps
- temporary verification symlinks
- cache folders created during testing

If ignore rules are missing, update `.gitignore` before staging.

Do not stage generated artifacts and then “remember to remove them later”.

### 6. Stage Only The Intended Scope

After `.gitignore` is correct and the replay is settled:

- stage only the files meant for the PR
- verify `.conduct` inclusion/exclusion again
- verify that no machine-local or generated artifacts are staged

Run:

```bash
git status --short
git diff --cached --stat
```

If a temporary verification helper was added, like a root `node_modules` symlink, remove it before commit unless it is intentionally part of the change.

### 7. Verify On The PR Branch

Run the relevant tests from the branch that will actually be pushed.

Do not rely only on tests run from the original worktree if the PR branch was rebuilt in a temporary worktree.

At minimum, run the tests that match the touched packages or the user’s requested verification scope.

### 8. Create Branch Name, Commit Message, PR Title, And PR Body From The Actual Diff

Branch naming:

- if a prefix is provided, prefix the branch name with it
- otherwise use a concise branch name that reflects the real change

Default branch pattern:

```text
<prefix>/<slug>
```

or, if no prefix is provided:

```text
codex/<slug>
```

Title rules:

- if a prefix is provided, prefix the PR title too
- mention the real primary areas changed
- do not collapse broad runtime work into a narrow feature label

Examples of what the title/body must capture when present:

- `datafn/swift`
- `datafn/swift-bridge`
- `searchfn/swift`
- example apps
- docs and regression coverage

Body rules:

- summarize the real change areas
- mention included packages/directories when the PR is broad
- list the tests actually run
- explicitly note `.conduct` inclusion or exclusion based on target

### 9. Push Using The Provided Remote Only

Derive the repository from the provided remote:

```bash
git remote get-url <target-remote>
```

Push the branch to that remote only.

Preferred approach:

- use the provided remote/repository
- use the `gh-other` auth context for PR creation
- if push permission is denied for that remote, stop and report the denial

Do not:

- add a new remote
- create a fork
- push to a personal repository
- silently change the destination repository

### 10. Create The PR And Verify The Live Metadata

Create the PR with:

- `GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other`
- the requested base remote + branch
- the pushed branch on the provided remote

After creation, immediately inspect the live PR:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh pr view <number-or-url> --json title,body,url,baseRefName,headRefName
```

Confirm that:

- the title matches the real scope
- the body reflects the actual work
- the correct remote/branch were used

If the live title/body are off, fix them before reporting success:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh pr edit ...
```

## Learnings To Carry Forward

- Check branch ancestry before doing anything else. An old branch can make a perfectly valid code change produce a terrible PR.
- Use a clean temporary worktree when the source branch is not a clean base for the target branch.
- Replay tracked file changes as patches whenever possible; full-file copying can wipe out newer target-branch fixes.
- Read enough of the changed files to describe the real work. Titles like “native-backed search” are wrong if the PR actually adds `datafn/swift` core runtime.
- Decide `.conduct` policy from the target branch up front, not at the end.
- Scan for ignore-worthy artifacts before staging. This is when `.build`, `.swiftpm`, `DerivedData`, `xcuserdata`, and verification symlinks are easiest to catch.
- Never stage temporary verification helpers such as `node_modules` symlinks.
- After PR creation, verify the live PR metadata. Do not assume the first draft title/body is good enough.

## Final Response Requirements

When the skill completes, report:

- PR URL
- pushed branch name
- target remote/branch
- whether `.conduct` was included or excluded
- whether `.gitignore` changed and why
- tests run on the pushed branch
- any abort reason if permissions or remote policy blocked completion

name: create-pr-ghother
description: Create or update a GitHub pull request using `GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other`, especially when the current worktree is dirty or based on the wrong branch. Use this when the user wants a PR against a specific remote and branch such as `origin/dev` or `next/next`, needs `.conduct` included or excluded based on target, wants branch/title prefixing, or needs a clean temporary worktree to avoid dragging unrelated history into the PR.
---

# Create PR GH Other

## Overview

Use this skill when the user wants a PR created with the `gh-other` GitHub profile and the result must be clean, accurately described, and targeted to a specific remote and branch.

This skill exists to avoid four recurring failure modes:
- pushing from the wrong branch ancestry
- creating vague or misleading PR titles and descriptions
- accidentally including `.conduct` content in the wrong target
- leaking generated/build artifacts because `.gitignore` was not checked before staging

## Required Inputs

- target remote and target branch
  - common: `origin/dev`
  - common: `next/next`
- optional prefix for both branch name and PR title
- the current worktree containing the intended changes

If the user gives only a branch name like `dev`, assume `origin/dev`.
If the user gives only `next`, assume `next/next`.

## Hard Rules

- Always set `GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other` on every `gh` command.
- Do not create forks.
- Do not create extra remotes.
- Push to the provided remote only.
- If permission is denied for that remote/repository, abort and report the denial. Do not fall back to a fork or a different remote.
- If the target is `origin/dev`, do not push `.conduct` contents.
- If the target is `next/next`, include `.conduct` contents.
- Before staging, scan the changed content for files that should be gitignored and update `.gitignore` first.
- Do not generate a PR title/body from guesswork. Read the actual changed files and make the title/body reflect the real scope.

## Workflow

### 1. Inspect The Current Worktree Thoroughly

Start by understanding what actually changed.

Run and inspect at minimum:

```bash
git status --short
git branch --show-current
git remote -v
git fetch <target-remote> <target-branch>
git rev-list --left-right --count <target-remote>/<target-branch>...HEAD
git diff --stat
git diff --name-status
```

Then read the high-signal changed files, not just filenames:

- source files
- tests
- examples
- docs
- package manifests
- `.gitignore`

Do this before drafting the branch name, commit message, PR title, or PR body.

### 2. Decide Whether A Clean Temporary Worktree Is Required

Use the current worktree branch only if it is already a clean PR base for the target branch.

Create a temporary clean worktree from `<target-remote>/<target-branch>` if any of these are true:

- the current branch is far ahead/behind the target branch
- the branch contains unrelated commits
- the user’s changes are mixed into an old branch
- a direct PR from the current branch would drag in unrelated history

When a clean worktree is needed:

1. create a temporary worktree from the target branch
2. replay the user’s intended changes into it
3. use that temporary worktree branch for commit, push, and PR

### 3. Replay Changes Safely

When replaying onto a clean worktree:

- For modified tracked files:
  - prefer patch-based replay over full-file copying
  - preserve upstream target-branch fixes
  - do not overwrite a newer target file wholesale unless the file is clearly example-only or entirely owned by the current change
- For brand-new files and directories:
  - copy them directly
- After replay:
  - run `git status --short`
  - confirm the staged/unstaged set still matches the intended scope

If replay causes conflicts or unexpected test regressions, resolve them before continuing. Do not silently ship the broken replay.

### 4. Apply `.conduct` Policy Before Staging

Target-specific policy:

- `origin/dev`
  - exclude `.conduct` contents from the PR
  - if needed, stage with explicit exclusions rather than hoping they stay out
- `next/next`
  - include `.conduct` contents

Do not decide this ad hoc. The target determines the policy.

### 5. Scan For Gitignore Candidates Before Staging

Before `git add`, inspect the full changed/untracked set for generated or machine-local files.

Check:

```bash
git status --short
git ls-files --others --exclude-standard
```

Common artifacts to catch:

- `node_modules/`
- `.build/`
- `.swiftpm/`
- `DerivedData/`
- `**/xcuserdata/`
- `**/*.xcuserstate`
- build outputs like `dist/`, `build/`, generated `.js`, `.d.ts`, source maps
- temporary verification symlinks
- cache folders created during testing

If ignore rules are missing, update `.gitignore` before staging.

Do not stage generated artifacts and then “remember to remove them later”.

### 6. Stage Only The Intended Scope

After `.gitignore` is correct and the replay is settled:

- stage only the files meant for the PR
- verify `.conduct` inclusion/exclusion again
- verify that no machine-local or generated artifacts are staged

Run:

```bash
git status --short
git diff --cached --stat
```

If a temporary verification helper was added, like a root `node_modules` symlink, remove it before commit unless it is intentionally part of the change.

### 7. Verify On The PR Branch

Run the relevant tests from the branch that will actually be pushed.

Do not rely only on tests run from the original worktree if the PR branch was rebuilt in a temporary worktree.

At minimum, run the tests that match the touched packages or the user’s requested verification scope.

### 8. Create Branch Name, Commit Message, PR Title, And PR Body From The Actual Diff

Branch naming:

- if a prefix is provided, prefix the branch name with it
- otherwise use a concise branch name that reflects the real change

Default branch pattern:

```text
<prefix>/<slug>
```

or, if no prefix is provided:

```text
codex/<slug>
```

Title rules:

- if a prefix is provided, prefix the PR title too
- mention the real primary areas changed
- do not collapse broad runtime work into a narrow feature label

Examples of what the title/body must capture when present:

- `datafn/swift`
- `datafn/swift-bridge`
- `searchfn/swift`
- example apps
- docs and regression coverage

Body rules:

- summarize the real change areas
- mention included packages/directories when the PR is broad
- list the tests actually run
- explicitly note `.conduct` inclusion or exclusion based on target

### 9. Push Using The Provided Remote Only

Derive the repository from the provided remote:

```bash
git remote get-url <target-remote>
```

Push the branch to that remote only.

Preferred approach:

- use the provided remote/repository
- use the `gh-other` auth context for PR creation
- if push permission is denied for that remote, stop and report the denial

Do not:

- add a new remote
- create a fork
- push to a personal repository
- silently change the destination repository

### 10. Create The PR And Verify The Live Metadata

Create the PR with:

- `GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other`
- the requested base remote + branch
- the pushed branch on the provided remote

After creation, immediately inspect the live PR:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh pr view <number-or-url> --json title,body,url,baseRefName,headRefName
```

Confirm that:

- the title matches the real scope
- the body reflects the actual work
- the correct remote/branch were used

If the live title/body are off, fix them before reporting success:

```bash
GH_CONFIG_DIR=~/.config/gh-other gh pr edit ...
```

## Learnings To Carry Forward

- Check branch ancestry before doing anything else. An old branch can make a perfectly valid code change produce a terrible PR.
- Use a clean temporary worktree when the source branch is not a clean base for the target branch.
- Replay tracked file changes as patches whenever possible; full-file copying can wipe out newer target-branch fixes.
- Read enough of the changed files to describe the real work. Titles like “native-backed search” are wrong if the PR actually adds `datafn/swift` core runtime.
- Decide `.conduct` policy from the target branch up front, not at the end.
- Scan for ignore-worthy artifacts before staging. This is when `.build`, `.swiftpm`, `DerivedData`, `xcuserdata`, and verification symlinks are easiest to catch.
- Never stage temporary verification helpers such as `node_modules` symlinks.
- After PR creation, verify the live PR metadata. Do not assume the first draft title/body is good enough.

## Final Response Requirements

When the skill completes, report:

- PR URL
- pushed branch name
- target remote/branch
- whether `.conduct` was included or excluded
- whether `.gitignore` changed and why
- tests run on the pushed branch
- any abort reason if permissions or remote policy blocked completion

name: composio-cli
description: Help users operate the published Composio CLI to find the right tool, connect accounts, inspect schemas, execute tools, subscribe to trigger events with `composio listen`, script workflows with `composio run`, and call authenticated app APIs with `composio proxy`. Use when the user asks how to do something with `composio`, wants to run a known tool slug, needs to discover a slug with `composio search`, fix a missing connection with `composio link`, inspect tool inputs with `--get-schema` or `--dry-run`, troubleshoot top-level CLI flows, or explicitly needs `composio dev` guidance.
---

<!-- AUTO-GENERATED: edit skills-src/composio-cli/index.ts and rebuild -->
<!-- release-channel: stable -->

# Composio CLI

## Default Workflow

1. Start with `composio execute <slug>` whenever the slug is known.
2. If several independent tool calls must happen at once, use `composio execute -p/--parallel` with repeated `<slug> -d <json>` groups.
3. If `execute` says the toolkit is not connected, run `composio link <toolkit>` and retry.
4. If the arguments are unclear, run `composio execute <slug> --get-schema` or `--dry-run` before guessing.
5. Reach for `composio search "<task>"` only when the slug is unknown. `search` accepts one or more queries, so batch related discovery work into a single command when useful.

- `--dry-run`: Preview the request shape without performing the action.
- `--file`: Inject a local file path into a tool that exposes exactly one uploadable file argument.
- `--parallel`: Execute multiple independent tool calls in the same invocation.
- `--account`: Select which connected account to use by alias, word_id, or account id when multiple accounts exist for the same toolkit.

- `--file` only works when the tool exposes a single uploadable file input. Otherwise use explicit `-d` JSON.

## `search` - Find The Slug

Use `search` only when the tool slug is not already known.

```bash
composio search "create a github issue"
composio search "send an email" --toolkits gmail
composio search "send an email" "create a github issue"
composio search "my emails" "my github issues" --toolkits gmail,github
```

- Batch related discovery work into one `search` invocation, then move back to `execute` once the correct slugs are known.

## `link` - Connect An Account

Use `link` when `execute` reports that a toolkit is not connected, or when the user explicitly wants to authorize an account.

```bash
composio link gmail
composio link googlecalendar --no-browser
```

Key flags:
- `--alias`: Assign an alias to the connected account. Required when creating an additional account for the same toolkit.

- Retry the original `execute` command after linking succeeds.

## `proxy` - Raw API Access

Use `proxy` when a toolkit supports a raw API operation that is easier than finding a dedicated tool slug.

```bash
composio proxy https://api.github.com/user --toolkit github --account work --method GET </dev/null
```

Key flags:
- `--account`: Select which connected account to use by alias, word_id, or account id.

## `run` - Scripting, LLMs, and Programmatic Workflows

For programmatic calls, loops, output plumbing, or anything beyond a single tool call, prefer `composio run`.

`composio run` executes an inline ESM JavaScript/TypeScript snippet with authenticated `execute()`, `search()`, `proxy()`, and the experimental `experimental_subAgent()` helper pre-injected. No SDK setup required.

Chain multiple tools:
```bash
composio run '
  const me = await execute("GITHUB_GET_THE_AUTHENTICATED_USER");
  const emails = await execute("GMAIL_FETCH_EMAILS", { max_results: 1 });
  console.log({ login: me.data.login, fetchedEmails: !!emails.data });
'
```

Fan out with Promise.all:
```bash
composio run '
  const [me, emails] = await Promise.all([
    execute("GITHUB_GET_THE_AUTHENTICATED_USER"),
    execute("GMAIL_FETCH_EMAILS", { max_results: 5 }),
  ]);
  console.log({ login: me.data.login, emailCount: emails.data.messages?.length });
'
```

Feed tool output into an LLM and get structured JSON back:
```bash
composio run --logs-off '
  const emails = await execute("GMAIL_FETCH_EMAILS", { max_results: 5 });
  const brief = await experimental_subAgent(
    `Summarize these emails and count them.\n\n${emails.prompt()}`,
    { schema: z.object({ summary: z.string(), count: z.number() }) }
  );
  console.log(brief.structuredOutput);
'
```

- Use top-level `execute --parallel` instead when the user only needs a few independent tool calls and does not need script logic.

## Auth

```bash
composio whoami   # check current session
composio login    # authenticate if whoami fails
```

## Escalate Only When Needed

If the user is stuck on top-level commands or needs fallback inspection commands, load [references/troubleshooting.md](references/troubleshooting.md).

If the user explicitly asks about developer projects, auth configs, connected accounts, triggers, logs, orgs, or projects, load [references/composio-dev.md](references/composio-dev.md). `composio dev` is not the default end-user path.

## Status

This is a proposed delivery model derived from the request. Exact current schema, API routes, UI components, and authorization helpers were not inspected for this backlog capture and must be verified before implementation.

## Current-state constraints

* Skillplane already has workspace tenancy, members, skills, visibility, authorization, audit, and immutable skill versions.
* Groups must not weaken existing workspace or skill authorization.
* Existing workspaces have no group records and must remain valid.
* Exact role capabilities and current API/MCP extension points are **not yet defined** in this thread.

## Proposed domain model

### skill_groups

Proposed fields:

* stable ID;
* workspace ID;
* name and optional description;
* normalized name for workspace-local uniqueness if uniqueness is desired;
* created/updated timestamps and actor attribution;
* archived timestamp.

### skill_group_skills

Proposed many-to-many association:

* group ID;
* skill ID;
* created timestamp and actor;
* unique constraint on group plus skill.

### skill_group_members

Proposed many-to-many association:

* group ID;
* workspace-member ID;
* created timestamp and actor;
* unique constraint on group plus member.

All associations must enforce the same workspace boundary transactionally. Foreign keys should not cascade-delete canonical skills, users, or historical audit evidence when a group is archived.

## Authorization model

**Required invariant:** existing workspace membership and skill visibility checks run before group behavior.

**Open question:** whether a group is organizational only or grants skill availability.

Recommended sequencing:

1. deliver organizational grouping with no authorization effect;
2. separately specify an explicit access-policy mode and precedence rules if group-based grants are required;
3. add explainability for effective access before enabling enforcement.

Potential administrators are workspace owners and admins, but the exact role matrix must be confirmed against current policy.

## API and MCP surface

**Proposal:** expose deterministic, paginated operations for:

* list/get/create/update/archive/restore groups;
* list group skills and members;
* add/remove skills and members idempotently;
* filter skill/member listings by group;
* optionally bulk-add/remove with bounded batch size and per-item results.

Exact route and tool names are **not yet defined**. Existing caller attribution, optimistic concurrency, idempotency keys, and audit conventions should be reused.

## UI boundaries

* Workspace settings: group lifecycle and membership management.
* Skill catalog: group filters and group badges.
* Skill detail: current groups.
* Member detail: current groups.
* Group detail: paginated skills, members, and recent changes.
* Empty, archived, unauthorized, and partial-bulk states require explicit designs.

## Data flow

1. Authorized actor selects a workspace and group operation.
2. Server resolves actor and workspace membership.
3. Server validates all referenced skill/member records belong to the workspace.
4. Transaction writes the group or association and durable audit event.
5. Read models/search indexes are refreshed or invalidated.
6. API returns canonical state; clients read back the result.

If groups later affect authorization, effective-access caches must be invalidated on every relevant membership or policy change.

## Reliability and concurrency

* Unique constraints prevent duplicate memberships.
* Add/remove operations are idempotent.
* Optimistic concurrency protects metadata edits and archive/restore races.
* Bulk operations use bounded batches and explicit partial results or a transactionally all-or-nothing contract.
* Pagination and stable ordering are required for large groups.
* Archive/restore behavior must be race-safe.

## Security and privacy

* Reject cross-workspace IDs even if the actor can access both workspaces.
* Do not expose private membership information through public skill discovery.
* Preserve least privilege for administration.
* Audit actor, operation, target IDs, source client, and outcome without storing secrets.
* If access-bearing groups are added, deny-by-default precedence and regression tests are required.

## Observability

Track:

* group and membership mutation outcomes;
* authorization denials;
* cross-workspace rejection attempts;
* bulk operation size and partial failures;
* query latency and cardinality;
* effective-access cache invalidation if introduced.

## Migration and compatibility

* Add nullable-independent tables; do not require backfilling existing skills or members.
* Existing queries retain current behavior when no group filter is supplied.
* No default groups should be inferred without an explicit product decision.
* Rollback should disable new surfaces and preserve inert group data for a future retry; avoid destructive down-migrations in production.

## Delivery sequence

### Phase 1: semantics and data contracts

* Decide organizational versus access-bearing behavior.
* Confirm role matrix, uniqueness, multi-group, archive, and personal-workspace rules.
* Define API/MCP contracts and audit events.

### Phase 2: persistence and domain services

* Add schema and constraints.
* Implement workspace-safe lifecycle and association services.
* Add unit, transaction, concurrency, and cross-workspace tests.

### Phase 3: read surfaces

* Add list/detail/filter APIs and indexes.
* Add UI group settings, group detail, and skill/member badges.
* Validate pagination, empty states, and accessibility.

### Phase 4: bulk and operational hardening

* Add bounded bulk workflows if required.
* Add metrics, audit views, failure recovery, and performance tests.

### Phase 5: optional access enforcement

* Only after a separate approved policy specification.
* Add effective-access calculation, explainability, cache invalidation, denial tests, and staged rollout.

## Validation

* Schema and migration tests.
* Domain invariants and duplicate/idempotency tests.
* Role matrix and cross-workspace denial tests.
* API/MCP contract tests.
* UI tests for create/edit/archive/filter and membership flows.
* Audit read-back verification.
* Performance tests for high-cardinality groups.
* Regression tests proving ungrouped workspaces retain current behavior.

## Risks and mitigations

* **Accidental access widening:** keep first release organizational or require explicit deny-by-default policy.
* **Role confusion:** distinguish roles, groups, and policies in UI and docs.
* **Large association sets:** paginate and bound mutations.
* **Stale discovery/access caches:** event-driven invalidation and read-after-write tests.
* **Destructive lifecycle behavior:** archive groups and preserve associations/history.

## Open questions

The product questions in the ideation document are blocking inputs for final architecture, especially access semantics, multiplicity, administrative roles, personal workspaces, and nesting.",

        "content": "Backlog issue: [SKI-12](<https://linear.app/21n/issue/SKI-12/support-git-hosted-skill-sources-and-repository-wide-imports>)

## Status

This is a proposed architecture based on the requested behavior and Skillplane's known immutable-version model. Exact repository services, database schema, provider abstractions, deployment topology, and UI code must be inspected before implementation.

## Current-state constraints

* Skillplane manages immutable skill bundles and published/candidate versions.
* Existing amendment policy controls review or trusted publication.
* Tenancy, visibility, authorization, audit, and contexts must remain authoritative.
* A mutable Git branch cannot replace immutable Skillplane version identity.
* Exact current Git integration capabilities are **not yet defined**.

## Proposed component model

### Git source registry

A workspace-scoped source record representing a repository and connection policy.

Proposed fields:

* source ID and workspace ID;
* canonical provider/repository identity and display URL;
* default ref strategy: pinned commit, tracked branch, or tracked tag;
* credential connection reference for private access, never a raw secret;
* discovery mode and optional manifest path;
* sync policy and current status;
* created/updated/archived timestamps and actor attribution.

### Skill source binding

Connects one managed skill to one path in a source.

Proposed fields:

* source ID and skill ID;
* repository-relative skill root or `SKILL.md` path;
* optional per-binding ref override;
* discovery key or upstream identity;
* last successful commit and content digest;
* drift/action state;
* unique constraints preventing ambiguous duplicate bindings.

### Sync run and per-binding result

Records one immutable synchronization attempt:

* requested ref and resolved commit SHA;
* trigger and actor;
* start/end timestamps;
* repository tree digest where useful;
* per-skill added/changed/unchanged/missing/conflict/error outcomes;
* candidate/version IDs created;
* sanitized provider diagnostics.

### Version provenance

Every source-created candidate/version should retain:

* source ID;
* repository identity and URL;
* resolved commit SHA;
* source path;
* source content/bundle digest;
* sync run ID;
* import actor and policy outcome.

## Synchronization pipeline

 1. Authorize the actor for the workspace and source.
 2. Resolve repository connection and credential reference.
 3. Resolve the requested branch/tag/commit to an exact commit SHA.
 4. Fetch a bounded tree or required paths through a constrained provider adapter.
 5. Discover skill roots deterministically.
 6. Validate paths, file types, sizes, manifests, bundle limits, and metadata.
 7. Build the canonical Skillplane file set without executing repository code.
 8. Compare source digests with current bindings and managed versions.
 9. Produce a preview: add, update, unchanged, missing, renamed candidate, or conflict.
10. On confirmed apply, create/import through existing immutable version and amendment-policy services.
11. Persist sync results and provenance transactionally where possible.
12. Read back created candidates/versions and update source health.

A no-op comparison must not create a new version.

## Single-file mode

* User supplies source, ref policy, and one `SKILL.md` or skill-root path.
* Validation confirms the path belongs to the resolved repository tree.
* The binding maps exactly one managed skill to that path.
* The Diffpanel example uses repository-relative path `skills/diffpanel-chapters/SKILL.md`; the canonical repository URL remains to be supplied.

## Repository-wide mode

**Proposal:** support a deterministic discovery precedence:

1. explicit repository manifest, if defined;
2. recognized skill metadata files;
3. bounded recursive discovery of `SKILL.md` roots.

The final convention is **not yet defined**. Discovery must preview every candidate and flag duplicate slugs, nested roots, unsupported bundles, and conflicting existing bindings.

One source detail endpoint/view returns all bindings with path, managed skill, resolved commit, digest, sync result, and drift state.

## Provider abstraction

Define a narrow interface for:

* canonicalize repository identity;
* verify access;
* resolve ref to commit;
* list bounded tree;
* fetch bounded blobs;
* register/verify webhooks if supported;
* expose rate-limit and retry metadata.

Initial provider selection is open. Public GitHub is a likely first candidate because the supplied collection example is GitHub-hosted, but this is a proposal, not a confirmed requirement.

## Security and supply-chain controls

* Never execute hooks, package scripts, binaries, or repository code.
* Reject absolute paths, traversal, symlink escape, unsafe submodules, unsupported media, and decompression bombs.
* Bound file count, per-file bytes, expanded bundle bytes, repository traversal depth, and total sync work.
* Treat manifests and Markdown as untrusted data.
* Store private-repository authorization as scoped credential references with rotation and revocation.
* Redact tokens and provider headers from logs and audit.
* Verify webhook signatures, timestamps, replay IDs, installation identity, and repository binding.
* Require workspace and skill authorization at both preview and apply.
* Preserve existing visibility rules; a public repository does not automatically make a managed skill public.
* Surface commit verification/signature information as evidence if available, without treating it as sufficient trust on its own.

## Concurrency and idempotency

* Key sync application by source, resolved commit, discovery configuration, and content digest.
* Use per-source serialization or optimistic concurrency to avoid racing webhook/manual runs.
* Make apply replay-safe after timeouts.
* Do not recreate successful candidates or bindings when recovering partial runs.
* For repository-wide sync, persist per-binding results so failed items can be retried without duplicating successful items.

## Rename and deletion handling

* Missing upstream paths mark bindings as action required; they do not archive or delete managed skills automatically.
* Rename detection may use explicit upstream IDs, manifest keys, or digest similarity, but requires confirmation when ambiguous.
* Source removal disconnects future synchronization while preserving immutable versions and provenance.
* Force-push or unreachable historical commits must be visible; previously recorded provenance remains immutable.

## API/MCP surface

**Proposal:** paginated, authorization-filtered operations for:

* create/get/list/update/archive/restore sources;
* validate connection and preview discovery;
* list source bindings and grouped skills;
* create/update/remove a binding;
* start/get/list sync runs;
* preview and apply repository-wide changes;
* filter skills by source and source status.

Exact tool/route names and least-privilege scopes are **not yet defined**. Long-running sync should use asynchronous jobs with status polling or events rather than holding a request open.

## Reliability and observability

Track:

* source access and auth failures;
* ref resolution latency and errors;
* provider rate limit and retry state;
* discovered/changed/unchanged/conflicting counts;
* no-op ratio;
* candidate/publication outcomes;
* webhook signature/replay failures;
* sync duration, queue age, partial failures, and recovery;
* drift age per binding.

Alerting should distinguish provider outage, expired credentials, malformed repository content, policy rejection, and internal persistence failure.

## Migration and compatibility

* Add source records and optional bindings without changing existing skills.
* Existing manual publish/amend flows remain authoritative and available.
* A manually managed skill is connected only through an explicit, confirmed operation.
* Define behavior for manual amendments to a source-bound skill before launch: reject, allow as divergence, or support overlays.
* Rollback disables synchronization and webhooks while preserving source records, bindings, runs, versions, and provenance.

## Delivery sequence

### Phase 1: source and provenance contracts

* Decide providers, ref policies, discovery convention, credential model, and manual-edit behavior.
* Define schema, provider interface, provenance, API/MCP contracts, and limits.
* Threat-model public and private source ingestion.

### Phase 2: public single-file source

* Implement public repository access, commit resolution, constrained file fetch, validation, preview, binding, and manual sync.
* Integrate changed content with existing amendment policy.
* Deliver source provenance on skill/version views.

### Phase 3: repository-wide discovery

* Add deterministic discovery and preview.
* Add bulk binding/apply with per-item idempotency and recovery.
* Deliver source detail and filter/group views.

### Phase 4: private sources and automation

* Add scoped credential connections and rotation.
* Add webhook and/or scheduled synchronization after deciding trigger policy.
* Add signature validation, replay protection, rate-limit handling, queues, and retries.

### Phase 5: hardening and ecosystem integration

* Load/performance tests for large repositories.
* Rename/transfer/fork handling.
* [skills.sh](<http://skills.sh>) integration only after its role and contract are defined.
* Operational dashboards, alerts, and recovery tooling.

## Validation

* Unit tests for URL canonicalization, ref resolution, path validation, discovery, digesting, and provenance.
* Contract tests against supported provider APIs.
* Security tests for traversal, symlinks, submodules, oversized files, malicious manifests, secret redaction, and webhook replay.
* Idempotency and concurrency tests for repeated/racing syncs.
* Integration tests from repository commit to candidate/version and policy outcome.
* Repository-wide partial-failure and recovery tests.
* Cross-workspace and private-source authorization denial tests.
* UI tests for source setup, preview, apply, source grouping, drift, and failure recovery.
* Production canary with a controlled public repository before broader rollout.

## Risks and mitigations

* **Supply-chain compromise:** immutable commit provenance, review policy, no execution, and visible diffs.
* **Credential leakage:** provider connections, least scopes, redaction, rotation, and audit.
* **Mutable refs/force-pushes:** resolve every run to a commit and preserve prior provenance.
* **Provider outages/rate limits:** queueing, backoff, status distinction, and manual retry.
* **Mass unintended changes:** preview, bounded batches, policy gates, and non-destructive deletion handling.
* **Layout ambiguity:** explicit manifest precedence and conflict states.
* **State divergence:** define manual-edit/overlay behavior before source binding launch.

## Open questions

Provider scope, ref semantics, trigger modes, repository layout, overlay behavior, rename/deletion policy, source transfer identity, and [skills.sh](<http://skills.sh>) integration are blocking design decisions for later phases.",

        "content": "Backlog issue: [SKI-11](<https://linear.app/21n/issue/SKI-11/support-skill-groups-and-workspace-member-assignments>)

## Context and motivating problem

Skillplane currently presents a workspace's skills without a domain grouping layer. A flat catalog becomes harder to navigate and administer as the number of skills and members grows. The requested capability is to group skills into areas such as Design, Marketing, Development, and Sales, then associate workspace members with the relevant groups.

This document captures product intent. It does not authorize implementation, staffing, or dates.

## Target users and stakeholders

* Workspace owners and administrators who organize skills and membership.
* Workspace members who need a focused view of domain-relevant skills.
* Skill authors and maintainers who need discoverability without duplicating skills.
* Security and operations stakeholders responsible for authorization and auditability.
* Agent clients that may eventually consume group-aware skill discovery through APIs or MCP.

## Core use cases

### Organize a domain catalog

An administrator creates a “Design” group, adds design-related skills, and sees the group as one coherent collection.

### Onboard a workspace member

An administrator associates a new designer with the Design group. The member can discover the skills relevant to that domain without searching the full catalog.

### Support cross-functional work

A member or skill may need to appear in more than one domain, such as Design and Marketing.

**Proposal:** model both relationships as many-to-many. This is not yet a confirmed decision.

### Audit and maintain groups

An administrator can inspect membership, understand who changed it, archive an obsolete group, and preserve historical evidence without deleting the underlying skills or members.

## Product principles

* Groups are workspace-scoped and cannot reference another workspace's records.
* Groups complement workspace roles; they do not replace owner, admin, editor, or viewer semantics.
* Membership is explicit. Skillplane should not infer it from titles, activity, or private data.
* Archive is preferred over destructive deletion when relationships or audit history exist.
* Existing workspaces remain valid with zero groups.

## Ideas discussed and product options

### Option A: organizational grouping only

Groups drive labels, navigation, filtering, and onboarding but do not change authorization.

* Lower security risk and simpler initial delivery.
* Does not solve cases where group membership is intended to grant access.

### Option B: group-based skill availability

A member's groups determine which workspace skills are available to them.

* Stronger delegation and least-privilege potential.
* Creates a new authorization layer and requires careful precedence rules.

### Option C: separate organization and access controls

A group organizes skills and members, while an explicit policy flag or separate access policy determines whether it grants availability.

* More expressive and safer long term.
* Higher conceptual and implementation complexity.

**Open question:** which option reflects the intended first release? The request supports organization and member association, but does not establish access-control semantics.

## Desired outcomes and success measures

* Administrators can create domain groups and maintain skill/member associations without duplicates.
* Members find relevant skills with fewer catalog searches.
* Group filters and detail views return consistent results across UI and API surfaces.
* No group operation leaks or links cross-workspace records.
* Group archival and membership changes remain auditable.
* Existing workspaces and skills require no migration action to continue working.
* If groups affect authorization, permission tests show no accidental access widening.

Potential quantitative measures are not yet defined. Candidate measures include time to onboard a member, skill discovery success, percentage of skills organized, and failed/unauthorized group mutations.

## Product and UX considerations

* Group names should be clear within a workspace; uniqueness rules need definition.
* Group cards or rows should show skill and member counts.
* Skill and member detail views should expose group membership.
* Filtering should support one or multiple groups if many-to-many is adopted.
* Empty groups should be valid during setup.
* Archived groups should disappear from normal selection while remaining recoverable.
* Bulk assignment may be important for large workspaces but should not obscure per-item failures.
* UI language must distinguish “workspace role,” “skill group,” and “access policy.”

## Operational considerations

* Every create, rename, archive, restore, and association change should be attributable.
* Bulk changes need bounded request sizes, idempotency, and clear partial-failure handling.
* Group membership counts and filters need pagination at scale.
* Support tooling should make effective membership and, if applicable, effective access explainable.

## Goals

* Workspace-level skill groups.
* Skill-to-group and member-to-group associations.
* Bidirectional inspection and filtering.
* Safe lifecycle and audit behavior.
* Explicit authorization semantics before production rollout.

## Non-goals

* Replacing workspace roles.
* Automatic group inference.
* Cross-workspace or organization-global groups in the initial scope.
* Nested group hierarchies unless separately approved.
* Automatic modification of skill content.

## Acceptance criteria

* Domain groups such as Design, Marketing, Development, and Sales can be represented.
* Authorized administrators can add and remove skills and members idempotently.
* Group, skill, and member views expose consistent associations.
* Search/list operations can filter by group.
* Cross-workspace associations fail safely.
* Archiving a group does not delete skills, members, or audit history.
* Existing ungrouped workspaces continue to work.
* Documentation and UI clearly state whether membership is organizational or access-bearing.

## Assumptions

* A workspace is the tenancy boundary.
* Existing skill and member identifiers remain canonical.
* Existing workspace roles continue to govern who may administer workspace configuration.

## Open questions

* Does group membership grant access, set defaults, or only categorize?

* Reusing existing `skill.json` metadata may cover some repositories.
* **Open question:** define a precedence order and preview before creating bindings.

### Update policy

* Auto-publish is fast but inappropriate for untrusted or broad changes.
* Existing Skillplane amendment/review policy can decide whether a changed source becomes a candidate or publication.
* **Proposal:** source sync feeds the existing policy instead of creating a parallel publishing path.

## Desired outcomes and success measures

* Teams can connect official Git skill files without maintaining duplicate source text.
* Every Skillplane version can show source repository, path, and commit provenance.
* Repository-scale sources expose a complete, filterable list of associated skills.
* No-op synchronization creates no duplicate versions.
* Sync failures are visible and recoverable without data loss.
* Import does not execute code or leak repository credentials.
* Existing publication review and authorization guarantees remain intact.

Candidate quantitative measures include sync success rate, drift duration, no-op rate, mean recovery time, duplicate-version count, and percentage of imported versions with complete provenance.

## UX considerations

* Source creation should validate URL, provider, access, ref, and discovery before saving.
* A preview should separate additions, updates, unchanged skills, removals, renames, and conflicts.
* Source status should distinguish connected, syncing, current, drifted, action required, auth failed, and unreachable.
* Skill detail should show source provenance and whether local edits or overlays are allowed.
* Source detail should group all associated skills and expose per-skill paths/results.
* Removing a source must explain that immutable skill history remains.

## Operational considerations

* Private-repository credentials require explicit scope, rotation, revocation, and redacted audit behavior.
* Provider rate limits, webhook replay, force-pushes, and deleted refs must be observable.
* Bulk sync needs concurrency limits, resumability, and per-skill results.
* Repository transfer or rename should preserve a stable source identity where possible.
* Source health must not be inferred solely from a successful webhook receipt.

## Goals

* Single-file Git source of truth.
* Repository-wide discovery/import for multiple skills.
* Common source grouping and provenance views.
* Deterministic immutable commit resolution.
* Secure, review-policy-aware synchronization.
* Non-destructive drift and failure handling.

## Non-goals

* Arbitrary repository code execution.
* General-purpose Git mirroring.
* Silent deletion when upstream content disappears.
* Assuming one repository layout.
* Replacing immutable Skillplane versions with mutable remote reads.

## Acceptance criteria

* Repository URL, ref policy, and skill path can configure a single binding.
* Each successful sync records commit SHA, path, digest, timestamp, and outcome.
* Repository discovery is deterministic and previewed.
* A source page lists all associated managed skills and statuses.
* Same commit plus content is idempotent.
* Changed content follows existing review/publication policy.
* Rename, deletion, malformed content, and conflicts are explicit and non-destructive.
* Untrusted-content boundaries prevent execution, path escape, oversized bundles, unsupported files, and secret exposure.
* Manual skills remain unchanged until connected.
* Source removal preserves immutable history.

## Assumptions

* Git repositories can be resolved through provider APIs or a constrained fetch layer.
* Current immutable bundle/version and amendment policy remain authoritative.
* A source and its bindings are workspace-scoped.

## Open questions

* Initial Git providers and authentication methods.
* Supported URL forms and self-hosted Git.
* Branch/tag/commit behavior.
* Manual, scheduled, or webhook sync triggers.
* Discovery manifest and directory conventions.
* Rename/deletion confirmation.
* Overlay or local-edit support.
* Repository fork/transfer identity.
* The role of [skills.sh](<http://skills.sh>): catalog, resolver, import partner, or reference only.",
